title: Can You Freeze Milk?

content_html:
Milk can be frozen, but it may separate or become slightly grainy after thawing because fat, proteins, and water do not always return to the same emulsion. It remains suitable when frozen before spoilage and thawed in the refrigerator, though texture may be better for cooking than drinking.

Leave room for expansion

Milk expands as it freezes. If using the original container, make sure there is headspace and the package is freezer-safe; otherwise transfer it to an appropriate container without filling it to the top.

Freeze portions you can use at one time

Dividing a large amount into smaller portions reduces thawing time and avoids repeatedly refreezing the same milk. Label each container with the date and amount.

Thaw in the refrigerator and shake well

Do not leave the container on the counter for hours. Thaw slowly under refrigeration and shake or whisk to redistribute fat; some texture separation may remain even when the milk is safe to use.

Do not freeze milk that is already spoiled

Freezing largely stops microbial growth but does not reverse spoilage that has already occurred. If milk already smells abnormal, has unexpected curdling, or spent too long unrefrigerated, freezing does not make it safe again.
